name: Local Models for Patient Data
title: Local Models for Patient Data
answer: Local models for patient data are machine learning systems deployed within a healthcare organization's own infrastructure, such as hospital servers, workstations, or approved edge devices, so that protected health information does not leave the organization's control. This includes models used for clinical documentation, imaging analysis, risk scoring, and operational tasks where patient identifiers are present. The scope covers both models developed in-house and third-party models that are installed locally rather than accessed through a vendor's cloud API. It also includes the surrounding controls for data storage, access, and audit logging that make local deployment a governance choice rather than only a technical one.

sections.body: Local models for patient data are machine learning systems deployed within a healthcare organization's own infrastructure, such as hospital servers, workstations, or approved edge devices, so that protected health information does not leave the organization's control. This includes models used for clinical documentation, imaging analysis, risk scoring, and operational tasks where patient identifiers are present. The scope covers both models developed in-house and third-party models that are installed locally rather than accessed through a vendor's cloud API. It also includes the surrounding controls for data storage, access, and audit logging that make local deployment a governance choice rather than only a technical one.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Local models for patient data typically run on servers or workstations inside a hospital or clinic network, often with dedicated graphics processing units for larger models and standard central processing units for smaller ones. The infrastructure includes container runtimes, model serving software, and local storage that holds both the model weights and any patient data used at inference time. Many deployments are placed in network segments that are isolated from the public internet, with access limited to clinical applications through internal interfaces. For smaller or remote sites, the same principle can be met with approved edge devices that process data on the device and send only de-identified or aggregated results onward.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins by selecting or building a model whose intended use matches a specific clinical task, then validating it on local patient data before any live use. In many cases, a base model is trained by a vendor or research group on non-local data, and the healthcare organization fine-tunes or calibrates it using its own de-identified or properly consented records. At inference time, patient data is passed to the local model through an internal application programming interface, and the model returns a result without transmitting the underlying record to an outside service. Routine monitoring compares model outputs against clinician judgment or reference standards to catch drift or performance gaps.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Governance for local models centers on proving where patient data went, who could access it, and which version of a model produced a given output. Organizations typically maintain a model inventory that records the source of model weights, training data lineage, validation results, and the clinical owner for each deployment. Access to the local inference service is restricted by role, and every request that includes patient data is logged so that an audit can reconstruct what the model saw and returned. Risk assessments cover both data protection obligations and patient safety, because a locally deployed clinical model can still cause harm if it is misconfigured, outdated, or used outside its validated population.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Local models for patient data are moving toward smaller, more efficient architectures that can run on modest hospital hardware without sacrificing clinical accuracy. Interest is growing in federated approaches where a model is improved across many sites without raw patient data leaving any one site, and in confidential computing that protects data even from the operator of the local infrastructure. As regulators and standards bodies clarify expectations for locally deployed medical AI, healthcare organizations are likely to treat local inference as one option within a broader set of controls rather than a complete answer to privacy or safety risk.
